idiom_name: Component interface + abstract Decorator holding a Component + concrete decorator subclasses
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define the Component interface, one ConcreteComponent, and an abstract Decorator that holds a Component reference, conforms to Component and forwards every operation to the held instance. Concrete decorators override only the operations they augment and fall back to the inherited forward for everything else, so wrappers stack in any order and clients keep using the Component type. Where the language offers delegation (Kotlin `by`, Go interface embedding, Python `__getattr__`, Ruby SimpleDelegator) the forwarding collapses into that mechanism and only the changed operations remain; without it the forwarding is written once in the abstract Decorator. Keep the interface narrow, because the forwarding cost is proportional to its width.
code_sketch:
Component c = new ConcreteComponent()
c = new LoggingDecorator(c)      # adds before/after the forwarded call
c = new RetryDecorator(c)        # stack order = combination
c.operation()                    # the client still sees Component
pitfalls: Changing the component interface: a decorator must preserve the contract it wraps — adding, removing, or renaming operations makes it an Adapter, breaking substitutability.
Forwarding drift: every operation that should pass through must be explicitly delegated; a forgotten pass-through silently drops behaviour; use a language delegation mechanism to make this mandatory.

Identity blindness: decorated objects are not the same object — instanceof/casts, identity comparisons (==), use as dict/hash keys, and serialisation break unless the decorator is explicitly designed to preserve or expose the wrapped instance.
Order-sensitive semantics: retry inside a cache retries the cached error; cache inside retry caches the retry attempt; the order is part of the contract and must be documented and tested.
Deep stacking: chains of five or more wrappers produce opaque stack traces, slow debug sessions, and cognitive overload; treat layering as a cost, not free extensibility.
Introspection breakage (Python): naive function decorators shadow the original __name__, __doc__, __signature__, and source location unless functools.wraps or an equivalent is applied.
Shared decorator instance across components: one decorator instance wrapping multiple components mixes per-component state; each decorated object needs its own decorator instance.
Over-specialisation: a decorator that only makes sense for one concrete component is not a decorator — it is special-casing that should live inside that component.

Wrong move: decorating some call sites and letting others use the raw component -> the guarantee the decorator promises (authorisation, rate-limit, audit) silently applies only to some entry points and the gap shows up as a production incident -> instead wrap once at the composition root so the decorator is the only path to the component.

Wrong move: sharing one decorator instance across many wrapped components as an optimisation -> per-component state (counters, caches, buffers) mixes across all of them and corrupts results -> instead give every decorated object its own decorator instance.

Wrong move: wrapping a hot-path function with a chain of naive decorators -> debuggers, profilers and APM/tracing tools report the wrapper's file, line and qualname instead of the real function and every layer adds a call frame, doubling call cost -> instead apply functools.wraps or wrapt, keep chains shallow on hot paths, and profile decorated code.

Wrong move: stacking decorators without recording the intended order -> a retry wrapped inside a cache retries a cached error while cache-inside-retry caches each retry attempt, and a later refactor silently flips the semantics -> instead assemble the stack in one factory or composition root and pin the order with an end-to-end call-order test.
